report.summary: Prior art includes automated red-teaming (Perez et al., 2022) where LLMs generate adversarial prompts, finding up to 30% attack success on earlier models but missing nuanced harms. Ganguli et al. (2022) reported harmful outputs in 10-20% of cases after RLHF. Multi-agent adversarial testing for harness hardening is less common; debated whether fan-out improves coverage or just creates redundant attacks. Self-attacking systems are underexplored but conceptually similar to automated red-teaming applied to the entire agent pipeline.
risks: Self-adversarial testing can miss novel attack vectors that the attacker models haven't been trained to generate.
Generating adversarial tests with the same model class may lead to blind spots if the harness shares vulnerabilities with the attacker.
Fan-out may amplify trivial bypasses rather than discovering fundamental flaws.
Real-world adversarial examples may differ from generated ones in distribution, leading to overconfidence in safety.
todos: Implement a self-adversarial test suite using a fan-out of attacker agents that attempt to bypass the egress fence via prompt injection, social engineering, and multi-step plans.
Measure bypass rate over time and monitor for novel attack patterns using a separate detector agent.
Incorporate known jailbreak templates as seeds and use LLM generalization to create variants.
Conduct regular human red-teaming to complement automated tests and catch overlooked attack types.

handoff.suggestion: Start with a simple implementation: spawn 10 attacker agents with instructions to exfiltrate a dummy secret, log all attempts, and train a classifier on successful bypasses. Run nightly and block any discovered patterns in the next deploy. Reference Perez et al. (2022) for methodology and Ganguli et al. (2022) for expected attack success rates. Keep the attacker models separate from the production system to avoid contamination.

name: q34-self-improving-gates
question: Systems that harden their own safety gates by attacking themselves: what prior art exists for using an agent fan-out as an adversarial test of the harness that runs it? What did such systems find, and what did they miss?
